title: Port field is silently overridden to 443 when it holds 8642 with an https:// host
body:
## Summary

`SavedConnection.normalizeHostAndPort` treats the value **8642** in the Port field as "no port supplied" and rewrites it to **443** whenever the Host field starts with `https://`. Because the Add-connection dialog pre-fills the Port field with `8642`, the Port field cannot express HTTPS on 8642 — the single value it is pre-filled with is the single value it cannot express. The only way through is to put the port in the Host field (`https://host:8642`), which is also what the README's HTTPS example happens to do, so this is easy to hit and hard to diagnose.

## How it presents

Tailnet setup where `tailscale serve` terminates TLS directly on 8642:

```
tailscale serve --bg --https=8642 8642     # https://host.tailnet.ts.net:8642 -> 127.0.0.1:8642
```

Add connection → Host `https://host.tailnet.ts.net`, Port `8642` (pre-filled), API Key set. The app probes the wrong port and reports e.g. `Gateway endpoint https://host.tailnet.ts.net/health returned ...` / "cannot reach"; `https://host.tailnet.ts.net:443` in this setup is a different service entirely. Entering `https://host.tailnet.ts.net:8642` in the Host field connects fine, and `/health` + `/v1/models` + `/api/sessions` all answer 200 from the published port — so the gateway is not at fault.

A related symptom when the scheme is wrong for the same reason: a plain-HTTP probe of a TLS listener answers `400 Client sent an HTTP request to an HTTPS server.`

Tailscale is a path this app advertises (README §"Connect remotely with Tailscale") and `tailscale serve` on the API-server port is the natural way to publish it, so HTTPS-on-8642 is a setup the app should be able to express.

## Where it is

`lib/core/models/connection.dart` — `normalizeHostAndPort`:

```dart
final normalizedPort = uri.hasPort
    ? uri.port
    : detectedHttps && fallbackPort == 8642
    ? 443
    : fallbackPort;
```

The `fallbackPort == 8642` arm is doing double duty: "the app's default" and "the user did not supply a port" are the same value, so a deliberate 8642 is discarded. The rule itself is intentional and locked in by a test (`test/connection_manager_test.dart`):

```dart
test('normalizes HTTPS URLs without an explicit port to 443', () {
  final normalized = SavedConnection.normalizeHostAndPort(
    'https://hermes.example.com',
    8642,        // <- the fallback *is* 8642, i.e. "absent"
  );
  expect(normalized.port, 443);
});
```

Reinforcing it, the dialog pre-fills that value (`lib/main.dart`):

```dart
_port = TextEditingController(text: (conn?.port ?? 8642).toString());
```

and `README.md` §"Connect over HTTPS" says "either include it in the URL (`https://host.example.com:8443`) or set the Port field to that value" — true for 8443, silently false for 8642.

## Proposed fix (PR to follow)

Make "no port supplied" an explicit state instead of a magic value, and let the field's blank state mean it — mirroring the idiom already used for the dashboard port (`_dashPort` defaults to `''`, parsed as `dashPortText.isEmpty ? null : int.tryParse(dashPortText)`, hint "Leave blank for default (9119)"):

1. `connection.dart`: `normalizeHostAndPort(String input, int? fallbackPort)`; when the Host field carries no port and `fallbackPort == null`, infer `443` for HTTPS and `8642` for HTTP.
2. `main.dart`: pre-fill the Port field blank for a new connection (the hint already names 8642), parse with `int.tryParse`, and pass `null` when blank.
3. `connection_manager.dart`: `saveConnection` / `updateConnection` take `int? port` and pass it through.

Net behaviour, all covered by tests:

| Host field | Port field | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `https://h` | blank | `https://h:443` (unchanged, #57's case) |
| `https://h` | `8642` | `https://h:8642` (**fixed**) |
| `https://h:8642` | anything | `https://h:8642` (already worked) |
| `h` | blank | `http://h:8642` (unchanged) |
| existing saved connection | pre-filled with its stored port | unchanged |

No migration concern for stored connections: editing one pre-fills the field with its saved port, so nothing is re-inferred.

## Design question for you

The alternative to the blank pre-fill is to keep the dialog pre-filling `8642` and track whether the field was edited (an `onChanged` flag) so an untouched default still means "absent". Same outcome, more state, and it keeps a value in the field that the user has to read as "maybe not a value". The PR takes the blank-default route because it deletes the `== 8642` comparison outright and matches how the dashboard port field already behaves — say the word if you prefer the flag instead and I'll rework it.

## Out of scope (not in the PR)

`SavedConnection.dashboardPort => dashboardPortOverride ?? (useHttps ? port : 9119)` means that in HTTPS mode the drawer screens assume the dashboard shares the gateway port; pointing them at a different port needs an explicit Dashboard Port. That is already configurable and this issue does not change it — mentioning it only because the same one-port assumption is what made the entry above confusing to read.

Happy to test against other setups (HF Spaces / Caddy on 443) if you want a second data point before merging.

title: fix: honour the Port field when it holds 8642 on an HTTPS host
body:
Fixes #110.

## What was wrong

`SavedConnection.normalizeHostAndPort` used the literal value `8642` in the Port field to mean "no port supplied":

```dart
: detectedHttps && fallbackPort == 8642 ? 443 : fallbackPort
```

The Add-connection dialog pre-fills that field with 8642, so the one value the field was pre-filled with was the one value it could not express: with an `https://` host you could not reach a TLS listener on 8642 — e.g. a `tailscale serve --https=8642` endpoint. The only way through was a port inside the Host URL. Editing an existing HTTPS connection on 8642 rewrote its port to 443 as well.

| Host field | Port field | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `https://host` | (blank) | 443 | 443 |
| `https://host` | `8642` | **443** | **8642** |
| `https://host` | `9443` | 9443 | 9443 |
| `host` | (blank) | 8642 | 8642 |
| `https://host:8642` | anything | 8642 | 8642 (URL wins) |

## Changes

- `lib/core/models/connection.dart` — `fallbackPort` is nullable; `null` means "not supplied" and infers the scheme default (443 for HTTPS, 8642 for HTTP). The magic 8642 comparison is gone.
- `lib/main.dart` — the Port field starts blank and its hint carries the default (`Leave blank for default (8642; 443 with https)`), the same idiom the dashboard port field already uses (`dashPortText.isEmpty ? null : int.tryParse`). A blank or non-numeric field now means "not supplied" instead of being coerced to 8642.
- `lib/core/services/connection_manager.dart` — `saveConnection` / `updateConnection` take `int? port`.
- `README.md` — the HTTPS section states the Port field rules, not just the URL rules.

## Verification

Clean checkout, CI-pinned Flutter 3.44.0 / Dart 3.12.0:

- `flutter analyze --no-pub --fatal-infos` → `No issues found!`
- `flutter test --no-pub` → `+1054: All tests passed!`

New tests: explicit 8642 on an HTTPS host at the normalizer and at `saveConnection` (asserts the resulting `baseUrl`), 8642 inferred for HTTP when blank, URL-port precedence, and 443 still inferred for HTTPS when blank.

Three existing tests used a literal 8642 to mean "no port supplied" (`connection_manager_test.dart` x2, `secure_connection_storage_test.dart` x1); they now pass `null` and keep their `443` assertions. To confirm the new tests actually hold the bug down, I re-ran the two touched test files with the old `8642 -> 443` shortcut reinstated: 110 pass, 2 fail — the two new regression tests.

## Behaviour change worth a second opinion

The Port field is blank by default on a new connection instead of pre-filled with 8642. Existing saved connections are unaffected — editing pre-fills the stored port. If you would rather keep the pre-fill, the alternative is tracking whether the field was edited and treating an untouched default as absent: more state for the same outcome, which is why I went with the blank field.

Not addressed here: `dashboardPort => dashboardPortOverride ?? (useHttps ? port : 9119)` still assumes an HTTPS deployment fronts the dashboard on the gateway port.

title: Leaving a chat mid-turn destroys the turn (dispose closes the SSE connection)
body:
## Summary

Leaving a chat while a turn is running **destroys the turn**. `_ChatScreenState.dispose()` calls `_client.close()` (`lib/core/screens/chat_screen.dart:460`), and `IOClient.close()` is `_inner.close(force: true)` (`http` 1.6.0, `io_client.dart:241`) — *"terminates all active connections"*. That aborts the in-flight SSE request, and the stock Hermes API server reads a client disconnect as an agent interrupt:

```
gateway/platforms/api_server_openai_routes.py:877
    await _abandon_agent_task(agent_ref, agent_task, "SSE client disconnected")
gateway/platforms/api_server.py:684 _abandon_agent_task()
    request_hard_interrupt(agent, reason, tool_reason=reason.lower())
```

Nothing restarts it. The turn's tool work is gone, and the transcript gains the server's placeholder row `Operation interrupted.` — which is exactly the text the app then renders, with no retry affordance and no indication that a *connection event*, not the model, ended the reply.

Server-side evidence (stock Hermes v0.21.5, session driven by this app over `/v1/chat/completions`):

```
12:12:57 INFO run_agent: Interrupt requested (hard): sse client disconnected
12:12:57 INFO ...api_server: SSE client disconnected; interrupted agent task chatcmpl-205d47b9...
12:12:57 INFO ...conversation_loop: Turn ended: reason=interrupted_by_system(sse_client_disconnected)
         model=deepseek-v4-flash api_calls=2/150 tool_turns=2 last_msg_role=assistant response_len=0
12:18:19 INFO run_agent: Interrupt requested (hard): sse client disconnected
12:18:19 INFO ...conversation_loop: Turn ended: reason=interrupted_by_system(sse_client_disconnected)
         api_calls=8/150 tool_turns=10 response_len=0
```

2 of the 5 turns in that session — the second after 8 model calls and 10 tool turns — died this way.

## Why it is not just "the user left, stop the work"

The Stop button already exists and is wired to `GatewayChatClient.cancelActiveMessage()`, which produces the same disconnect deliberately. Leaving the screen is not a stop request, and everything the app does around turns says the turn should survive: it polls authoritative history after a lost socket (`_pendingReattachResync`, "the server keeps the turn running detached"), it has a whole durable-turn/recovery stack, and it shows the *Background recovery unavailable — legacy transport* banner precisely because it wants durable turns.

## Reproduction

1. Open a chat on a stock Hermes server (legacy transport), send a prompt that runs tool calls for a while.
2. Press back to the session list while the turn is still streaming.
3. Watch the gateway log: `SSE client disconnected; interrupted agent task …`.
4. Reopen the chat: the last row is `Operation interrupted.`, the work is gone.

Worth noting `#92` assumed "the turn completes server-side, the client just misses the final message" — against stock Hermes it does not complete; it is interrupted.

## Proposed fix (PR incoming)

Do not manufacture a disconnect on dispose: hand the live stream to a detached closer and close the HTTP client once the stream settles. Screen callbacks already guard on `mounted`, so a detached stream is safe. `GatewayChatClient` gains `isStreaming` / `whenStreamSettles()`.

This removes one cause of the mid-turn kill. The other causes are outside the app's control (screen lock / Doze, network handover, proxy recycling an idle connection) and are tracked upstream — `NousResearch/hermes-agent#85016` (api_server SSE disconnect hard-kills the turn; PRs #117230 opt-in `X-Hermes-Detached-Stream`, #96507 detach on disconnect). Until one lands, a killed turn is unrecoverable, so a follow-up could offer an explicit "the connection dropped and the server cancelled this turn — Continue" affordance rather than rendering the placeholder as if it were the answer.

title: fix: keep a running turn alive when the chat screen is disposed
body:
Fixes #112.

## What was wrong

`_ChatScreenState.dispose()` closed the screen's HTTP client. `IOClient.close()` calls `_inner!.close(force: true)` (`http` 1.6.0, `lib/src/io_client.dart:243`) — *"terminates all active connections"* (same file, line 235) — so leaving a chat mid-turn aborted the in-flight SSE request. The stock Hermes API server reads a client disconnect as an agent interrupt. Line numbers below are measured against the gateway driving this app, Hermes `v0.21.5+4538.g7728574`:

```python
# gateway/platforms/api_server_openai_routes.py
_write_sse_chat_completion() :966   await _abandon_agent_task(agent_ref, agent_task, "SSE client disconnected")
_write_sse_responses()       :1013  await _abandon_agent_task(agent_ref, agent_task, "SSE client disconnected")

# gateway/platforms/api_server.py
_abandon_agent_task()        :708   request_hard_interrupt(agent, reason, tool_reason=reason.lower())
```

Both call sites sit in an `except (ConnectionResetError, ConnectionAbortedError, BrokenPipeError, OSError)` around the SSE writes: the interrupt fires when the next write to the abandoned socket fails, which is exactly what a `force: true` client close produces.

The turn and its tool work were destroyed server-side and the transcript gained the server's `Operation interrupted.` placeholder. Measured against that gateway over `/v1/chat/completions`: 2 of the 5 turns in one session ended `reason=interrupted_by_system(sse_client_disconnected)`, the second after 8 model calls and 10 tool turns with `response_len=0` — from `~/.hermes/logs/agent.log`:

```
12:12:57 Interrupt requested (hard): sse client disconnected
12:12:57 Turn ended: reason=interrupted_by_system(sse_client_disconnected) api_calls=2/150 tool_turns=2 response_len=0
12:18:19 Interrupt requested (hard): sse client disconnected
12:18:19 Turn ended: reason=interrupted_by_system(sse_client_disconnected) api_calls=8/150 tool_turns=10 response_len=0
```

## Change

- `GatewayChatClient.isStreaming` / `whenStreamSettles()` — exposes the live stream's settle point. The per-send completer is settled on **every** exit from a send (in `finally`, before `_liveStream` is cleared), not just the ones that reach the SSE subscription: a `send()` that fails before the response headers, an abort that races the response, and a non-200 reply all leave the client's socket finished with, so a detached closer must not wait out the backstop on them.
- `chat_screen.dart` — dispose hands the stream to a detached closer: the client is closed once the stream settles, not while a turn is streaming. The screen's callbacks already guard on `mounted`, so a detached stream cannot touch disposed UI, and a 30-minute backstop releases the client if a stream never settles.
- Deliberate cancellation is untouched: the Stop button still goes through `cancelActiveMessage()`, which is the disconnect the server is *supposed* to read as a stop.
- The client being closed is this screen's own — `_ChatScreenState` builds a per-screen `ApiClient` (`chat_screen.dart:355`) and `ApiClient._http` is `httpClient ?? _freshClient()`, so no other screen or in-flight request shares it.

## Tests

`test/chat_dispose_stream_lifecycle_test.dart` — six widget tests:

- keeps the SSE connection open while the turn is streaming, and closes it once the stream settles
- closes the detached client when the stream fails
- closes the client on dispose when no turn is streaming
- releases the client when a stalled stream never settles
- releases the client when the request dies before any reply (the send fails before the response headers)
- releases the client when a non-200 reply outlives the screen

Proven to bite, both ways:

- with the pre-fix dispose reinstated, 3 of the 4 original tests fail (`Expected: false / Actual: <true>` — the client was closed while a turn streamed), while the idle-screen test still passes;
- with the settlement coverage removed again, the two failure-exit tests fail (`Expected: true / Actual: <false>`) and the other four pass.

Gates (run locally at the Flutter 3.44.0 / Dart 3.12.0 the workflow pins):

- `flutter analyze --no-pub --fatal-infos` -> `No issues found!`
- `flutter test --no-pub` -> `+1055: All tests passed!`

## Scope

This fixes the legacy REST/SSE transport (the branch `submit` takes when there is no Desktop Gateway). The Desktop Gateway paths — `_sendRecoverableGatewayMessage` and `_sendDesktopGatewayMessage` — are not affected and stay as they are: that transport closes its socket mid-turn on dispose deliberately, and the gateway does not cancel the running turn for it (`close_on_disconnect` defaults to `false`; a single-client WS disconnect goes through the one teardown path in `tui_gateway/session_lifecycle.py`), which is what the app's turn coordinator and journal recovery rely on.

Causes outside the app (screen lock / Doze, network handover, an intermediary recycling the connection) still end the turn, because the server interrupts on the disconnect and nothing restarts it: tracked upstream as `NousResearch/hermes-agent#85016`. A follow-up could surface an explicit *"the connection dropped and the server cancelled this turn — Continue"* affordance instead of rendering the placeholder as if the model had answered.

title: fix(voice): expose TTS engine via manifest queries, fix proxied dashboard auth
body:
## Summary

Fixes two user-visible silent failures in the Hermes Android client. Both
fail without any error surfaced to the user.

**1. Spoken replies (TTS) produced no audio at all.**

The manifest declared the STT package query (`android.speech.RecognitionService`)
but not TTS. Since Android 11 (API 30) package visibility is restricted by
default, so `flutter_tts` could not resolve the system TTS engine and `speak()`
failed silently into an existing `catch`. Speech-to-text input worked; the
answer was mute. Adds `android.intent.action.TTS_SERVICE` to `<queries>`.

**2. Settings/Cron/Memory/Skills returned HTTP 401 when "Dashboard behind proxy" was on.**

`_authHeaders()` returned a bare `Content-Type` for any proxied client, so a
stored API key or username/password was never sent. That is correct only when
upstream infrastructure really injects auth; on a direct LAN dashboard it
breaks every route. Stored credentials are now always sent, and the proxied
flag only suppresses them when the client has neither an API key nor a
password. The toggle subtitle now warns to leave it OFF on a direct LAN
dashboard.

## Also included

This branch additionally carries the author's local release work on top of
upstream `v2.1.8` (Android Auto wiring: method channel, foreground service,
receivers, manifest declarations; a dashboard API-key bearer fallback; a
desktop-gateway opt-in; release signing path). Reviewers wanting only the two
fixes above should look at the final commit, `a39c8d3`.

## Test plan

- [x] `flutter analyze` clean (two pre-existing warnings in `auto_messaging_service.dart`, unrelated)
- [x] Release APK builds and is signed with the release key
- [ ] On-device: "Play test sentence" in Settings speaks audible audio
- [ ] On-device: Settings opens without 401 on a direct LAN dashboard

title: [P0] server→client requests not advertised: clarify / approval / secret never reach the phone
body:
**Client:** **v2.1.8** — commit `9025361089ceb41f27d3d6ca8c393b2e98d157c5` (annotated tag object `8e006344113427868f03ddce1fc4b6f79b0a54b1`), `app-arm64-v8a-release.apk`
**Severity:** blocking for any human-in-the-loop Hermes workflow from the phone

## Summary

Against a Hermes Agent `0.21.5` host, this client never advertises
`client.capabilities {server_requests: true}`, so the server fails fast on every server→client request
(`clarify`, `approval`, `secret`, `sudo`, vault prompts, …). The clarify tool returns immediately with an
empty answer and the agent is told nothing was answered. The official web client against the same host
renders the same question interactively and returns the answer, so this is client-side compatibility,
not a host limitation.

## Environment

**Host (Hermes server)**
- Hermes Agent `0.21.5` — `GET /health` → `{"status": "ok", "platform": "hermes-agent", "version": "0.21.5"}`
- OS: Windows 11; `hermes dashboard --host <TAILSCALE_IP> --port 9119 --no-open --skip-build` (profile `default`, single profile)
- Gateway API Server: `127.0.0.1:8642` (loopback-only), exposed to the tailnet with a local TCP forward `<TAILSCALE_IP>:18642 → 127.0.0.1:8642`
- Dashboard auth provider: username/password (basic-auth provider), reached over **plain HTTP** on a Tailscale address (both apps allow cleartext)
- Transport to phone: Tailscale (Android client, Including split-tunnel mode)

**Phone / client**
- Android device: Android 17
- Network: 5G mobile data, Tailscale connected (app added to the split-tunnel include list)


## Minimal reproduction

1. Connect the app to the host above (Gateway API port `18642`, dashboard 9119 + username/password).
2. Open a small/new session.
3. Send exactly: `请用 clarify 工具问我一个二选一问题，选项给 A 和 B 两项`
4. Watch the app and the host log at the same time.

## Expected

The app renders the question with its choices, the user answers, and the agent receives that answer
(the same interaction the official web client performs against this host).

## Actual

- The app shows only a generic tool-activity row (`Clarify`), with no question and no options.
- The tool returns instantly, with an empty answer; the agent then reports it received no answer.
  (Observed agent output: `clarify 已发出并返回，但结果是空的：user_response: ""`.)
- The host logs, verbatim:

```
2026-10-01 22:17:53,941 INFO [20261001_221651_5c7538] tui_gateway.server_requests: server request clarify for c5e81cf5 not sent: the attached client predates server→client requests (update the Hermes app)
```

## Working control (same host, same credentials, same minute)

Official dashboard web client, loaded in the phone's browser from the same host:
the identical clarify prompt rendered as an interactive list and the answer was accepted end-to-end:

```
) "web端首条测试"是要我在哪个网页端发送/验证第一条测试内容？
  ▸ 1. ChatGPT 网页端（推荐）(Recommended)
    2. 你当前正在开发的网页应用
    3. 其他网页端（请说明）
    4. Other (type your answer)
0/1 answered · ↑/↓ select · Enter confirm and continue · Esc/Ctrl+C cancel
→ ChatGPT 网页端（推荐）(Recommended)
```

The shipped web bundle contains the capability advertisement the server keys on
(`web_dist/assets/api-*.js`: `client.capabilities` and `server_requests:!0`).

## What the Hermes 0.21.5 contract currently says

From the host's own `tui_gateway/AGENTS.md` (verbatim):

> A client says once per connection that it answers them (`client.capabilities {server_requests: true}`,
> sent by the shared channel on `gateway.ready`); a WebSocket client that never did is an app build older
> than server→client requests, and `send()` fails fast for it instead of stalling the agent for the deadline.

Other properties of the same contract, for reference:

- Server→client request methods currently registered: `clarify`, `approval`, `secret`, `sudo`,
  `vault.code`, `vault.save_login`, `vault.unlock_prompt`, `preview.read`, `preview.act`,
  `terminal.read`, `window.read`, `tour`.
- Requests carry `srq-<n>` ids and block the agent thread until the matching response frame arrives.
- `open_requests(sid)` is replayed on `session.resume` / `session.events.since`, so a reconnecting client
  is expected to re-render still-open questions.
- The desktop client reaches the same server over WebSocket via `apps/shared` (`JsonRpcGatewayClient`).

## Impact

Not a cosmetic degradation: the phone cannot participate in any Hermes workflow that needs a human
decision. The agent does not stall — the request is dropped and the tool returns empty — so a phone user
can be silently bypassed on approvals rather than merely blocked.

## Notes for the maintainer

- We are not prescribing an implementation; the contract above and the two host log lines are the
  verifiable facts.
- If this client shares its gateway/Wire layer with other transports, the same one-line
  `client.capabilities` advertisement likely fixes all of them.

## A note that may shorten the fix

This app already ships clarify/approval/secret UI and models for its Desktop-Gateway path —
`lib/core/models/gateway_clarify.dart`, `gateway_approval.dart`, `lib/core/widgets/gateway_clarify_dialog.dart`,
`gateway_approval_dialog.dart`, `chat_screen.dart` (dialog wiring), and
`GatewayTurnPendingInput.allowedKinds = {'approval','clarify','secret','sudo'}` in
`lib/core/models/gateway_turn_contract.dart`. What is missing is the *advertisement* on the dashboard/gateway
WebSocket and the plumbing from standard server→client request frames into those existing widgets. We are not
prescribing an implementation — this is only to say the UI layer appears to already exist, so the gap may be
narrower than it looks.

## Extra evidence: the client is identifiable in the host's access log

Requests from this app arrive with the User-Agent `Dart/3.12 (dart:io)` (26 requests captured during the
session above), which makes it easy to correlate client requests with the server-side auth/WS events while
you reproduce.

title: Large sessions: session restore is coupled to a full transcript fetch, so a big/slow transcript makes the chat unusable
body:
**Client:** **v2.1.8** — commit `9025361089ceb41f27d3d6ca8c393b2e98d157c5` (annotated tag object `8e006344113427868f03ddce1fc4b6f79b0a54b1`)
**Severity:** blocking with large sessions; a slow link is an amplifier, not the root cause

## Summary

With a session whose rendered transcript is ~2.1 MB, this client:
1. shows `Failed to load messages / TimeoutException after 0:00:20.000000: Future not completed`, and
2. cannot send — tapping the image attachment surfaces `JsonRpcError(session.resume): Timeout`.

Both come from the same design: the client ties *session attach* to a *full-history fetch*.
The host's protocol does not require that, and we measured the difference on the host itself (below).

## Environment

**Host (Hermes server)**
- Hermes Agent `0.21.5` — `GET /health` → `{"status": "ok", "platform": "hermes-agent", "version": "0.21.5"}`
- Windows 11; `hermes dashboard --host <TAILSCALE_IP> --port 9119` (single profile `default`), reached over
  **plain HTTP on a Tailscale address**; Gateway API on `127.0.0.1:8642`, exposed to the tailnet via a local
  forward `<TAILSCALE_IP>:18642 → 127.0.0.1:8642`

**Phone / client**
- Android device: Android 17
- Network: 5G mobile data through Tailscale (app included in split-tunnel), measured path ≈ 400–800 ms RTT
  and 2–22 KB/s at the time of these reports


## Minimal reproduction

Real-world (what we hit, and what any user hits on a slow link):

1. Open a session whose rendered transcript is ~2.1 MB / ~4,261 rows (the host reports both; ours was a
   long-running chat).
2. The chat shows `Failed to load messages / TimeoutException after 0:00:20.000000: Future not completed`.
3. Tap the image/attachment button while that state is up → the picker is suppressed, and a send attempt
   fails with `JsonRpcError(session.resume): Timeout`.

Deterministic variant, if you want it without a slow network: delay the transcript response for one session by
more than 20 s. Note honestly: `tools/fake_gateway` has a slow-path idiom but **not** a transcript-delay switch
today — the slow path is driven by prompt text (`"slow stop test"` → `asyncio.sleep(10.0)`,
`fake_gateway.py:503/532/870/1220`), so this would need a small local delay added to the transcript handler
(or client-side network throttling). We did not want to present it as a ready-made switch.

## Expected

Opening a large session should attach the session (state, run status, pending prompts) and let the user keep
talking while history hydrates asynchronously; a history failure should not make the session unusable.

## Actual

- `ApiClient.requestTimeout = Duration(seconds: 20)` is applied to the transcript GET with no windowing,
  so a large payload on a slow link can never complete inside the deadline.
- `session.resume` is issued without any of the host's documented light-attach options, so the reply carries
  the **entire rendered transcript**, which the client then discards — and the chat screen fetches the same
  history again over REST (the payload is paid for twice).
- The same 20 s deadline is used for that resume, so on a slow link the resume result times out.

## Code pointers (v2.1.8)

| Where | Fact |
|---|---|
| `lib/core/services/connection_manager.dart:635` | `static const Duration requestTimeout = Duration(seconds: 20);` |
| `lib/core/services/connection_manager.dart:703-716` | `getMessages()` → `GET /api/sessions/<id>/messages` with `.timeout(requestTimeout)`, no `limit`/`order` |
| `lib/core/services/ws_client.dart:959` | `send('session.resume', {'session_id': sessionId})` — no `omit_messages`, `lazy`, `defer_history`, `inline_images` |
| `lib/core/services/ws_client.dart:959-995` | `ResumedGatewaySession` keeps only `session_id`, `running`, `status`, `inflight`; the `messages` array in the same reply is parsed and dropped |
| `lib/core/screens/chat_screen.dart:874-918` | `_fetchMessages()` sets `_loading = true` and stores the error as the chat's error state |
| `lib/core/screens/chat_screen.dart:1361-1362` | `_showAttachmentPicker()` returns early while `_loading` |
| `test/api_client_timeout_test.dart` | the fixed timeout is deliberate and covered by a test |

## What the Hermes 0.21.5 contract offers (documented, verifiable)

`tui_gateway/contracts/sessions.py` — `SessionResumeParams` includes `lazy`, `defer_history`,
`omit_messages`, `eager_build`, `close_on_disconnect`, and `inline_images` (its comment: *"False: render image
parts as \"[image]\" instead of their data URIs — a remote client reads a transcript in kilobytes instead of
re-transmitting every stored attachment"*). With `omit_messages` the reply still carries `message_count`,
`running`, `status` and `inflight` (`tui_gateway/methods_session.py:812-830`), and the resume guard loads the
TIP segment only (`methods_session.py:766-775`).

### Measurements we ran against this host (loopback = healthy path, so no network excuse)

| Call | Reply size | Time |
|---|---|---|
| `session.resume` for a 272-message session, current client style (no options) | **5,522,686 B** (1,820 rendered messages) | 1.01 s |
| same session, `omit_messages: true` | **2,617 B** (`messages_omitted: true`, `message_count: 272`) | 0.17 s |
| `session.resume` for a 735-message session, no options | **21,595,795 B** (6,785 rendered messages) | 5.01 s |
| same session, `omit_messages: true` | **2,618 B** (`message_count: 735`) | 0.20 s |
| `GET /api/sessions/<id>/messages` (272-message session) | 1,307,647 B | 0.06 s |
| same, `?limit=50&order=latest&profile=default` | **367,988 B** (50 rows) | 0.02 s |

So: attach can be ~2.6 KB and the transcript fetch can be windowed; today the client does neither, and on a
slow link every one of those full transfers must fit in a fixed 20 s.

## What we are *not* claiming

- Not claiming the network is irrelevant: at 2–22 KB/s a 2.1 MB fetch cannot finish in 20 s. That is exactly
  why the coupling is the problem — the session should not be hostage to it.
- Not claiming the WebSocket transport is at fault, and not asking for "a longer timeout" as the fix;
  a longer timeout is only a diagnostic stopgap.
- We are not prescribing an implementation. The contract facts, the code pointers and the measurements above
  are the whole claim.

## Impact

A user with a real, long-lived session cannot open it or send anything from the phone when the link is slow —
the session is effectively lost from the mobile client, on a host that is perfectly healthy.

title: fix: handle gateway server-to-client requests
body:
## Summary

- advertise `server_requests` capability after `gateway.ready`
- handle server-to-client JSON-RPC requests for clarify, approval, sudo and secret prompts
- reply with the original string request ID and use `clarify.lock` for batch questions
- replay `open_requests` after session resume and dismiss cancelled prompts without stale responses
- retain the legacy event and response paths for older gateways

## Root cause

Hermes now sends interactive prompts as server-to-client JSON-RPC requests with `srq-*` IDs. Android only recognised notification events and responses to its own integer IDs, so these requests were silently dropped and the UI never received the prompt.

## Tests

- `flutter analyze lib/core/services/ws_client.dart lib/core/services/desktop_gateway_client.dart lib/core/screens/chat_screen.dart test/ws_server_requests_test.dart test/connection_manager_test.dart`
- `flutter test test/ws_server_requests_test.dart`
- `flutter test test/connection_manager_test.dart`
- `flutter test test/gateway_approval_test.dart test/gateway_clarify_test.dart test/gateway_sensitive_prompt_test.dart`
- `git diff --check`

Closes #116

title: fix: keep large sessions usable during history load
body:
## Summary

- resume gateway sessions with `omit_messages`, `defer_history`, and `inline_images: false` so attaching does not transfer a full rendered transcript
- fetch only the latest 50 transcript rows through the REST pagination contract
- keep the remote composer, voice input, and attachment picker usable while visible history is loading
- ignore a late history response after a remote turn starts so it cannot overwrite optimistic or streamed messages
- use the same bounded history fetch for reconnect recovery and post-turn refreshes

## Root cause

Android paid for the complete transcript twice: once inside `session.resume`, where it discarded the returned messages, then again through an unbounded REST request. Both paths shared a 20-second deadline, and the composer was disabled while the REST request was pending. Large sessions on a slow link could therefore time out during both attach and history loading, leaving the chat unusable.

## Tests

- `flutter analyze lib/core/services/ws_client.dart lib/core/services/connection_manager.dart lib/core/screens/chat_screen.dart test/connection_manager_test.dart test/large_session_restore_test.dart`
- `flutter test` (1,061 tests passed)
- `git diff --check`

Closes #117

title: Recovery v2: submitting from an existing server-side chat forks a brand-new session (`session.open` has no existing-session target)
body:
**App version:** v2.1.8 · **Gateway:** a stock Hermes backend implementing the accepted v2 contract (behaviour matched against `tools/fake_gateway/turn_recovery_contract.py`)

**Status:** confirmed against a self-hosted Hermes server that advertises the capability (`session.open` / `turn.reconcile` / `turn.interrupt` live; also reproduced after a server restart, where the lost binding made a reconnect mint yet another session). Related: #84 (capability absent upstream → fallback), #87 (app sessions not persisted) — this issue is the behaviour once a server DOES implement the contract.

## What happens

`ChatScreen` routes **every** submit through the recovery coordinator whenever the gateway advertises `capabilities.turn_recovery` (`lib/core/screens/chat_screen.dart:1960` — `_sendMessage`; the coordinator is also opened from `_initializeChat` via `recoverPending`):

- `localSessionId` passed to the coordinator is `widget.session.id` (`chat_screen.dart:2360`, `:2421`).
- For chats loaded from the server session list, `Session.id` **is the server's stored session id** (`lib/core/models/session.dart:41` `Session.fromJson`; navigation at `session_list_screen.dart:937/1557`, `workspace_screen.dart:103`).
- The coordinator mints a fresh `mobile_session_id` per local chat (`gateway_turn_coordinator.dart:801`) and `session.open` carries **only** that id: the contract has no way to tell the server which existing session to bind (the reference fixture forbids client session targets — `tools/fake_gateway/turn_recovery_contract.py:488`, `client_session_authority_forbidden`).

A contract-compliant gateway therefore **creates a new stored session** for such a chat. Observed on a real gateway: opening a chat that already existed server-side and sending a message produced a brand-new empty session; the turn ran there while the app kept reading/writing the chat's original transcript (`storedSessionKeyFor(widget.session.id) ?? widget.session.id`, `chat_screen.dart:1091`). The message shows live, then disappears on the next reload; the server accumulates duplicate sessions.

A follow-up reconnect can also fail the binding: the app's journal expects `stored_session_id` to stay stable across opens (`gateway_turn_contract.dart:443-445`), but a contract-correct server answers with the session it minted for that `mobile_session_id` (a new one whenever the binding row was lost), which lands in the `invalidBinding` path.

## Repro (against a gateway implementing the contract)

1. Create a chat from another client (Desktop/CLI) so it exists server-side.
2. Open that chat in the Android app and send a message.
3. Inspect the gateway: the message went to a newly created session; the chat's original transcript is untouched; the app's next reload shows the old transcript without the new message.

## Expected

Submitting from an existing chat should either stay on that chat's session, or the app should not use the recovery route for chats it cannot bind to (falling back to the live transport), instead of silently forking.

## Suggestions (app side)

- Skip the recovery route when `widget.session.id` is already a stored session id (use the live/desktop transport for those chats), **or**
- adopt the existing stored id as the coordinator's `mobileSessionId` for such chats so the binding resolves to the same session on first open, **or**
- extend the contract with an explicit bind method (e.g. `session.bind {stored_session_id}`) validated server-side — today the fixture deliberately forbids client-chosen session targets.

*(Static analysis of v2.1.8 plus confirmed reproductions on a real server; a contract-level test that persists sessions — beyond the synthetic ledger — would pin the behaviour.)*

title: fix(sessions): use Gateway is_active for liveness instead of ended_at
body:
## Problem

The session list (Chats tab and project session lists) showed **finished sessions as "Running"**.

`Session.fromJson` derived `isActive` from `ended_at == null`. But the Gateway only sets `ended_at` for **explicitly ended** sessions — a chat that has finished its turns but was never ended keeps `ended_at: null` forever. So every completed-but-not-ended session rendered as live: the Chats browser showed a "Running" chip and the workspace session list showed `Running`.

## Fix

Read `is_active` — the Gateway's actual liveness flag — first, and fall back to the `ended_at` heuristic only when it is absent (older gateways):

```dart
final isActiveJson = json['is_active'];
...
isActive: isActiveJson is bool ? isActiveJson : (endedAt == null),
```

## Verification

- **On-device (Android 15 emulator, real gateway)**: with `is_active: false` sessions, the Chats list now shows no "Running" chip and the Home digest shows "Idle"/"Done" — before the fix every finished session rendered as running.
- **Regression tests** (`test/session_model_test.dart`): both directions — `is_active: false` + `ended_at: null` → idle; `is_active: true` → active. The `project_sessions_tree_test.dart` helper now omits `is_active` by default so the legacy fallback stays exercised.
- `flutter analyze --no-pub --fatal-infos` → clean
- `flutter test --no-pub` → **1069/1069 pass**

title: fix: keep existing Gateway sessions on target
body:
Fixes #120

## Summary

- distinguish local chat drafts from sessions loaded from the Gateway
- reserve recovery v2 `session.open` for local drafts
- route existing server sessions through the legacy transport that targets their exact session ID
- prevent the legacy client from eagerly creating a second session while recovery v2 owns a local draft
- retain safe legacy establishment after an explicit recovery-v2 fallback

## Validation

- `flutter analyze --no-pub`
- `flutter test --no-pub` — 1,076 tests passed
- focused session-model, new-chat, and turn-recovery tests — 42 passed
- independent focused review approved the final routing and fallback call chain

title: fix(sessions): treat un-ended but stale sessions as idle
body:
## Problem

`Session.fromJson` treats `is_active` as the session-liveness signal, but the Gateway API does not actually send it — the session serializer's stable keys end at `last_active` (verified against Hermes 0.21.5 and current `main`). The fallback therefore decided liveness from `ended_at` alone, and because sessions that finish their work are never explicitly ended, every old chat kept showing as running in the Chats tab, Projects, and the session list.

## Fix

Mirror the Hermes dashboard's definition of an active session (`_ACTIVE_WINDOW_S = 300` in its sessions router): an un-ended session is live only while `last_active` is within five minutes. The agent stamps `last_active` at least once a minute while a turn is in flight (`SESSION_ACTIVITY_HEARTBEAT_MIN_INTERVAL_SECONDS = 60`), so the window cannot miss live work.

- `kSessionActiveWindowSeconds` documented in the session model
- `is_active` (should a future gateway send it) still wins
- ended sessions are never active, regardless of recency

## Tests

- un-ended + recent activity → active (recency fallback)
- un-ended + stale activity → idle (the regression)
- ended + fresh activity → still idle
- `flutter analyze --no-pub --fatal-infos` clean · `flutter test --no-pub` 1078/1078 pass

title: feat(android): declare per-app language support (localeConfig)
body:
## What

The app ships nine catalogues (#115 / v2.1.11) but never declared `android:localeConfig`. Per the platform docs, omitting that manifest entry signals that users should not be able to set the app's language independently of the system language — so Android 13+ system settings deliberately omit the per-app language picker.

## Changes

- `android/app/src/main/res/xml/locale_config.xml` — the nine shipped locales (`en`, `ja`, `zh-Hans`, `ko`, `es`, `fr`, `de`, `pt-BR`, `ru`), with English as the ultimate fallback.
- `android/app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml` — `android:localeConfig="@xml/locale_config"`.

## Result

On Android 13+ users can pick the app's language independently: **Settings → Apps → Hermes Agent → Language** (or **Settings → System → Languages & input → App languages**). The selection flows through the existing Flutter resolution added in #115 (`resolvePreferredLocale`), so `zh-Hans` / `pt-BR` map to the right catalogues and everything else falls back to English.

## Verification

- Release build compiles with the declaration (`flutter build apk --release`).
- The per-app locale mechanism already drives the app UI (validated on-device during the localization work with the same system mechanism).

title: fix(theme): keep bottom bar labels on a single line
body:
## What

The bottom navigation bar lets its labels wrap onto two lines. In Japanese the Activity destination — アクティビティ, seven glyphs — overflows its destination slot at the 12sp label ramp and breaks as アクティビ / ティ.

Measured on a Pixel 7 emulator (3x density, five destinations at 72dp each): the label renders ~198px wide against the ~183px that actually fits, while プロジェクト (six glyphs, 183px) just fits — hence exactly one label wraps.

## Change

`navigationBarTheme` in `hermesTheme`:

- 11sp, `letterSpacing: 0`, `height: 1.2` — fits the widest shipped label on one line.
- Selected/unselected colors preserved (`onSurface` / `muted`), so the bar looks unchanged otherwise.

This is a widget-level fix rather than a shorter Japanese string: German (`Aktivitäten`), Portuguese, and Russian entries are the same length class, so they get the same protection.

## Verification

- Pixel-measured before/after on the emulator: the second-line fragment is gone and all five labels render on one line (ja).
- `flutter analyze` clean; `flutter test` 1104/1104.

title: feat(chat): copy part of a message via a select-text dialog
body:
## What

Copying a message always takes the whole thing; there is no way to grab just one sentence. This adds a **Select text** action to the message sheet (right below Copy message) that opens the message in a selection-enabled dialog.

## How it works

- The dialog renders the message with the same markdown style as the bubble and `selectable: true`, so long-pressing starts a selection with the platform handles and toolbar (Copy / Share / Select all).
- The bubble's long-press actions are untouched — selection lives in the dialog instead of fighting the existing long-press gesture.
- A Close button dismisses the dialog.

## i18n

`select_text` added to all nine catalogues (en, ja, zh-Hans, ko, es, fr, de, pt-BR, ru) plus the generated localisations.

## Verification

- New widget test: long-press → Select text → the dialog shows selectable text → Close dismisses it. 1105 tests pass, `flutter analyze --fatal-infos` clean.
- On a Pixel 7 emulator (ja): long-press a message → テキストを選択 → long-press inside the dialog → the selection toolbar appears → Copy → pasting into the composer yields only the selected word, not the whole message.

title: feat(notifications): desktop-parity notification kinds and settings
body:
## What

The app only posted "turn completed" notifications. This brings the mobile client up to the desktop app's notification model: **seven kinds behind per-device toggles, four prioritized channels, notification actions, and tap routing.**

| Kind | Source | Channel |
|---|---|---|
| Approval needed | approval requests (with **Approve / Deny buttons**) | Attention (high, heads-up) |
| Input needed | clarify / sudo / secret prompts | Attention |
| Response complete | turn settled | Turns |
| Turn failed | failed or fail-closed turn | Turns |
| Background task complete | background completions | Background (low) |
| Credit notifications | `credits.depleted` / `credits.restored` notices | Notices |
| Plugin notifications | other gateway notices | Notices |

All of them fire only while the app is in the background (the phone is away), and the desktop's 1s replay throttle is mirrored.

## Structure

- **`notification_prefs.dart`** — master switch + per-kind toggles, persisted per device (`SharedPreferences`), read synchronously by the dispatcher.
- **Service** — `showKind` maps kind → channel/importance, applies prefs + throttle; `showTurnFailed` joins `showTurnCompleted`; `sendTestNotification` bypasses gating so a silent OS-level block can be told apart from a dead feature.
- **Wiring** — the chat screen mirrors approvals (approve/deny actions, payload carries session + request id), clarify/sudo/secret prompts, turn failures, background completions, and credit/plugin notices.
- **Settings** — a Notifications section: master, seven kind toggles (disabled while the master is off), Send test notification, and a hint when Android blocks notifications.
- **Tap + action routing (app root)** — approval buttons answer through the turn controller (the same path as the in-app dialog); every response opens the session the notification was about, falling back to the workspace.
- **l10n** — 23 new keys across all nine catalogues.

## Verification

- `flutter analyze --fatal-infos` clean; **1122/1122 tests pass** (+17 new: prefs store, kind/channel/importance/action mapping, gating, throttle, failed-turn and approval wiring).
- On a Pixel 7 emulator (ja): the Notifications section renders all seven kinds; the Android 13+ permission dialog appears; **Send test notification posts a real notification — verified visible in the notification shade** ("Hermes 通知テスト").

## Notes

Killed-app delivery (push) stays out of scope, per the roadmap's "real native architecture" item.

title: Model picker should work in API-server-only mode without requiring Dashboard :9119
body:
## Summary

The Android model picker currently depends on the Dashboard endpoint/port (`:9119`) even when the app is otherwise working correctly in API-server-only mode over `:8642`.

In my setup, Hermes Android and Hermes Desktop can use the same session concurrently when Android is connected only through the Hermes API server on `:8642`.

However, opening the model picker tries to reach `:9119` and fails if the Dashboard is not running.

If I enable `:9119` so the model picker works, the Android app starts using the Dashboard/Desktop-Gateway path and the session becomes owned/locked by that side, preventing the Desktop client from continuing the same session.

This defeats the main reason for using the `:8642` path.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent: `v0.21.5+7025.g27c02f6 (2026.9.24)`
- Hermes Agent commit: `27c02f6326e82b2ba184f5a849f0c5b3a38efb9c`
- Native Windows 11 host
- API Server: `0.0.0.0:8642`
- Dashboard / Remote Gateway: intentionally disabled during normal use

## Reproduction

1. Run Hermes with the API server enabled on `:8642`.
2. Do **not** run the Dashboard on `:9119`.
3. Connect Hermes Android to the API server.
4. Open an existing chat/session.
5. Chat normally.
   - This works.
   - The same session can remain usable from Hermes Desktop at the same time.
6. Tap the model selector.

Observed error:

```text
Could not load models for this profile:
ClientException with SocketException:
Connection refused ...
uri=http://<host>:9119/
```

7. Start the Dashboard on `:9119`.
8. The model picker can now load.
9. However, Android now uses the Dashboard/Desktop-Gateway path, and in this setup the session becomes locked/owned by that side, so Desktop can no longer continue writing to the same session.

## Root cause in current Android code

In `lib/core/screens/chat_screen.dart`, when no `DesktopGatewayClient` is configured, `_showModelSelector()` falls back to `_modelListingClient()`.

`_modelListingClient()` still constructs a `DashboardClient` using `widget.connection.dashboardPort`, and then calls:

- `GET /api/model/info`
- `GET /api/model/options`

So "no Desktop Gateway" still implicitly requires the Dashboard port for model selection.

## Why this should be possible over :8642

Current Hermes Agent API Server already exposes model/session control endpoints on `:8642`, including:

- `GET /api/model/options`
- `POST /api/sessions/{session_id}/model`
- `GET /api/sessions/{session_id}`
- `GET /v1/capabilities`

`/v1/capabilities` advertises both:

- `model_options`
- `session_model_lock`

This appears sufficient to support model selection without enabling the Dashboard transport.

## Suggested behavior

When Hermes Android is operating in API-server-only / REST fallback mode:

1. Load available models from `GET /api/model/options` on the API Server (`:8642`).
2. Read the current session model from session metadata/current chat state instead of requiring `/api/model/info` from the Dashboard.
3. Apply the selected model using:

   `POST /api/sessions/{session_id}/model`

4. Keep the app on the existing `:8642` transport rather than implicitly requiring or activating `:9119`.

## Expected result

The model selector should work in a valid `:8642`-only configuration.

Users should not need to enable the Dashboard on `:9119` just to list or change the model, especially when enabling that path changes session ownership behavior and prevents seamless Desktop + Android use of the same session.

title: fix: support model picker in API-server-only mode
body:
## Summary

Fixes #129.

title: feat(chat): keep composer drafts per session and refresh session chips
body:
## What

Two rough edges from daily use:

1. **Leaving a chat lost the draft.** Whatever you typed vanished when you backed out of a chat (or the app was killed). Composer drafts now persist per session in `SharedPreferences` (device-local): saved on dispose and on app pause, restored on open. The share-sheet prefill still wins when present, and empty text clears the entry so a sent message cannot resurrect as a draft.

2. **Running/idle chips went stale.** The session lists fetched once on open, so a chat you just messaged kept showing its old state until a manual pull. The lists now refresh silently every 10s while visible (injectable interval; tests drive loads explicitly) and cancel the timer on dispose.

## Verification

title: Chat header shows Unassigned despite confirmed server-side Project membership
body:
## Summary

The Android chat header displays **Unassigned** for a chat that the live Hermes backend correctly places in a Project. This is a UI metadata inconsistency, not a missing project folder or a failed server-side assignment.

## Reproduction and observations

1. Open an existing Project that has a valid primary folder on the gateway host.
2. Create a new chat from within that Project and send a unique test message.
3. Inspect the chat header: the reporter's screenshot shows **Unassigned**.
4. Independently inspect the same stored session on the live backend:
   - `sessions.cwd` matches the Project's primary folder.
   - The first tool-environment snapshot already uses that folder.
   - `projects.tree` includes the exact stored session ID in the intended Project's `sessionIds`, not in the synthetic Home bucket.
   - `projects.for_cwd` returns the intended Project.

No session move or folder change was performed during this test. The screenshot and server results refer to the same uniquely titled test chat. The exact installed APK version has not yet been collected, so I am not claiming reproduction on the latest release.

## Expected behavior

The header should display the server-resolved Project name and stay consistent with server-side placement after creation, session-ID reconciliation, and reopening a chat.

## Actual behavior

The chat runs in the correct Project folder and is filed under that Project by the server, but its header says **Unassigned**.

## Relevant source path / suspected cause

Inspected source at commit `534a33a9e59ffb886246e7360613821f3085e95b`:

- `lib/core/screens/chat_screen.dart`, around line 3538: `ChatContextHeader(projectName: widget.projectName, ...)`.
- `lib/core/widgets/chat_context_header.dart`, lines 42 and 59–61: an empty/null `projectName` is rendered as Unassigned.
- `projectName` is constructor/navigation metadata in `ChatScreen`; the header does not derive it from the current gateway session/project response at this call site.

This explains how missing or stale navigation metadata can disagree with authoritative backend placement. The exact navigation transition that drops the label still needs a client-side regression test; it was not captured on the reporter's device.

## Suggested fix and regression coverage

Resolve/reconcile the displayed Project from authoritative session/project metadata after create/resume and stored-session-ID mapping, rather than relying solely on the initial widget argument. Preserve the distinction between unknown/loading metadata and genuinely unassigned placement.

Please cover creation within a Project, reopening from the general chat list, and draft-to-stored session-ID reconciliation with widget/integration tests.

Related to #100, but distinct: that issue concerned an unsupported assignment RPC preventing chat creation. Here creation and cwd-based server filing succeed; only the displayed Project label is wrong.

title: feat(chat): mid-turn steering via session.steer, plus filing/assets/batch features
body:
## Summary

Adds **mid-turn steering** to the chat screen plus several related features and fixes, all behind the existing desktop-gateway transport:

### Mid-turn steering (`session.steer`)
- Composer stays editable while a turn streams; a steer button sends the text via the gateway's `session.steer` RPC so it lands in the agent's live turn (same contract as the desktop app).
- If the gateway rejects the steer (turn settling), the text is held and re-sent as a normal prompt when the turn settles — including when the user is dictating (drain defers until the mic stops, so the "will be sent next" promise never silently no-ops), and when the user presses Stop (stop drains the held steer).
- Steered messages render with a **STEER** chip; the marker survives reloads by parsing the gateway's persisted `display_kind: "steer"` / `[OUT-OF-BAND USER MESSAGE]` projection (regex verified byte-exact against `prompt_builder.format_steer_marker`, with a fallback for transports that omit `display_content`).
- Dictation stays enabled during streaming (voice is the hands-free steer path); steering mid-dictation finalizes the transcript first so partials are never sent and the recognizer never writes into a cleared composer.
- Input row stays usable at 320/360/800dp at text scale 1.0/1.3: inert buttons (attach, spoken-replies toggle) hide mid-turn to keep the composer >120dp; Stop also silences an in-flight spoken reply.

### Other commits on this branch
- AI-assisted filing UI consuming the gateway `filing.*` contract.
- Assets gallery backed by the gateway `assets.*` index (per-project gallery).
- Batch pin/unpin/archive with undo in the chat lists (partial batch stays undoable; capability probes deduped).
- Live tok/s estimate in the streaming status banner.
- Review fixes on the above (filing/batch/assets).

## Test plan
- [x] `flutter test` — 1156 tests pass (new: steer RPC/UI, steer chip history parsing, dictation×steer race regressions, streaming input-row layout at 5 size/scale combos with negative controls)
- [x] `flutter analyze --fatal-infos` clean

title: feat(chat): render MEDIA: refs as gateway file cards
body:
## What
Renders the gateway's `MEDIA:/path` delivery tags as interactive file cards in assistant bubbles instead of dead prose.

- **Parser** (`lib/core/utils/media_tags.dart`): ports the desktop `parts.ts` semantics — anchored paths (`/`, `~/`, `X:\`), quoted captures, trailing-punctuation shedding, streaming guard (partial paths stay prose until a deliverable ext lands), 58-ext parity with the gateway's `MEDIA_DELIVERY_EXTS`.
- **Cards** only for refs occupying their own line (the gateway's canonical delivery form); mid-line refs become inline markdown links wired to the same download+share action, so lists/tables never fragment.
- **Card widget**: downloads via the gateway `fs/download` RPC (never the local filesystem), share sheet with proper MIME types, inline image preview (decoded at cacheWidth 1080), coalesced concurrent downloads, state reset on ref change.
- Code fences are split before parsing — `MEDIA:` examples inside fences stay verbatim, including mid-stream unclosed fences.

## Audit
Deep audit (3 parallel auditors: state machine, wire contract vs gateway+desktop, UI regressions) found and fixed: markdown fragmentation, unclosed-fence card leak, ext-list drift (18 missing exts silently dropped archive/geo/presentation cards), unkeyed-state clobbering on streaming ref growth, double-tap no-op, temp-file hygiene, full-res image decode. Verified clean: history persistence keeps tags verbatim (cards survive reload), no catastrophic regex backtracking, dispose guards.

## Tests
24 parser/widget cases in `test/media_tags_test.dart`; full suite 1180 pass; `flutter analyze --fatal-infos` clean.

**Stacked on #134** — the first 14 commits are that PR's; this diff narrows to the 4 media commits once #134 squash-merges.

title: feat: offer the newest GitHub release at launch
body:
## What does this PR do?

Adds an in-app awareness of new builds: when the app opens normally it asks GitHub Releases for the newest published build of `rusty4444/hermes-android`, and if there is one the user has not skipped, it offers to open that release. The app never downloads or installs anything itself — the release page is where the APK lives, and the system browser is the path to it.

Today an install sits on whatever version it was side-loaded with until the user remembers to go and look at the releases page.

## How it behaves

- **Plain launches only.** A launch that already has something to do — a share intent, a Quick Chat shortcut — is not interrupted with a dialog.
- **At most twice a day**, and the request is conditional (`If-None-Match`), so an unchanged release answers `304` and costs nothing against GitHub's per-IP budget for unauthenticated callers.
- **Silent when there is nothing to say**: switched off, checked recently, current, previously skipped, or GitHub unreachable. A launch is never blocked, slowed, or given an error by this check.
- **`Skip this version`** remembers the *version*, and stays quiet until something newer than that ships. **`Later`** asks again at the next launch.
- **Settings → About** gains `Check for updates` — a real check with an honest answer (`You’re on the latest version.` / `Couldn’t check for updates.`) — and a `Check for updates on launch` switch, default on.
- A request that **never reached GitHub** (offline, DNS, timeout) does not consume the throttle: the next launch retries. An *answered* failure (403 rate limit, 5xx, malformed payload) does, because that request did spend the budget.

## Where it lives

| file | what |
|---|---|
| `lib/core/services/app_update_service.dart` | the check, the version comparison, the throttle/skip policy (`launchPromptRelease`), and the preference |
| `lib/core/widgets/update_available_dialog.dart` | the prompt: release, version, notes, and the three actions |
| `lib/core/screens/workspace_screen.dart` | the post-frame launch hook, plus injectable `updateService` / `installedVersionLoader` seams |
| `lib/core/screens/settings_screen.dart` | the two About-card entries |
| `lib/l10n/*` | 10 new strings in all 11 catalogues, with the regenerated `app_localizations_*.dart` |

The prompt renders the release notes with `flutter_markdown` — already a dependency, as are `http`, `shared_preferences`, `package_info_plus` and `url_launcher`. **No new packages.**

## Version comparison

Tags are `v2.1.19`; `package_info` reports `2.1.19` for a `2.1.19+2159` build, so both shapes are normalised before comparing. The comparison is dotted-numeric, with a missing segment read as zero (`2.2` == `2.2.0`) and a pre-release suffix sorting *below* the release it precedes — so a `-beta` tag never prompts a stable install to "update" to it.

## How to test

1. `flutter test --no-pub test/app_update_service_test.dart test/update_available_dialog_test.dart test/workspace_update_prompt_test.dart`
2. `flutter analyze --no-pub --fatal-infos`
3. On a device: open the app while the published release is newer than the installed build → the prompt appears; `Skip this version` silences it until something newer ships. Settings → About → `Check for updates` answers immediately, whatever the state.

## Tests

**34 new tests** in three files:

- `test/app_update_service_test.dart` (22) — version ordering and normalisation (including the pre-release and `+build` cases); newer / equal / `304` / `403` / malformed / draft responses; the throttle, including that a check which never reached GitHub is retried next launch; ETag storage; the whole launch-prompt policy (off, skipped, newer, current, unreachable); skip bookkeeping.
- `test/update_available_dialog_test.dart` (6) — what renders (release, version, notes; the tag as the label when a release has no title) and each action, including a launcher that throws.
- `test/workspace_update_prompt_test.dart` (6) — the shell end to end against a fake GitHub: a plain launch prompts; `Later` asks again at the next launch (the shell is unmounted between launches so the hook genuinely re-runs instead of being skipped by element reuse); `Skip this version` silences that version; no prompt when current, when package_info cannot answer, or on a share launch.

**Proven to bite** — each behaviour reverted on its own, then restored:

| revert | failure |
|---|---|
| launch hook never fires | `workspace_update_prompt_test.dart`: `a plain launch prompts when a newer release is published` fails |
| skip list ignored | the skip tests fail in both the service file and the wiring file |
| throttle window never closes | `throttles repeat checks but honours a forced one` fails |
| an equal version counts as newer | `reports up to date when the published release is not newer` fails |
| dialog never reaches the launcher | `View release opens the release page and reports it` fails |

## Gates

```
flutter analyze --no-pub --fatal-infos   # No issues found!
flutter test --no-pub                    # 1268 passed (1234 before this change; 34 added)
```

Read `docs/CHECKLIST.md`: it is scoped to release PRs, so no CHANGELOG entry here.

## Notes for review

- The repo has no spec for an update mechanism (`docs/` has no mention of one), so the behaviour above is my judgement call: advisory, twice-daily, switchable off, and never able to block a launch. If you would rather it checked every launch, or always prompted instead of honouring a skip, that is a one-line change in `launchPromptRelease`.
- The check is unauthenticated, like any anonymous client of the GitHub API. A token would raise the rate limit, but it would have to live in the APK, so I did not add one.
- `test/workspace_update_prompt_test.dart` stubs the installed version (`installedVersionLoader`) because `package_info` has no platform channel under `flutter test`; everything else in that test is real, including the service and the HTTP client.

title: fix(chat): close a batch clarify card only once
body:
## What

Answering one question of a batch clarify request closed its card twice and navigated the user out of the conversation, so the remaining questions could only be answered by leaving the chat and coming back. A cancellation arriving while an answer is in flight closed a second route the same way.

## Why

A `clarify` server request can carry up to five questions (`params.questions[]`, each with a `qid`). Answers lock one at a time through `clarify.lock`, and `DesktopGatewayClient.respondToClarify` emits `clarify.remaining` for the questions still open **before** the call that was answering returns.

So when the user submits an answer from a card, two things close the same route:

*   `GatewayClarifyDialog._respond` pops with `true` on success, and
*   `_reconcileClarifyPrompts` sees that card's question leave the remaining set and pops it as well.

The surplus pop lands on whatever route is underneath — the chat screen (the user is navigated out of the conversation), or the next question's card when it has already been opened. In debug builds it trips `Navigator._debugLocked`; on device the next question's card cannot be submitted until the chat is re-entered, which replays it as the only remaining question.

The same surplus pop has a second trigger. If `request.cancel` arrives while `clarify.lock` is pending, the cancellation closes the card itself and the queue drains — the next question's card can open — while the answer callback is still awaiting its lock. When that lock resolves (the gateway reports `status: expired`, which `respondToClarify` treats as a successful result) the card pops a route it no longer owns. `mounted` is still true during the closing animation, and `Route.isCurrent` stays true through the `pop`/`popping` lifecycle phases, so neither is a guard.

## Changes

*   `lib/core/screens/chat_screen.dart` — a prompt the user answered from its own card is recorded as self-answered for the duration of the send, and `_reconcileClarifyPrompts` leaves that route alone: the reconcile exists for questions resolved elsewhere (a cancellation, another route). The record is consumed once the card's route closes, because the flat, non-batch clarify shape never emits `clarify.remaining`. A new `_ownsClarifyPromptRoute` answers "the open card still belongs to this prompt" — `_clarifyPromptRouteOpen` plus the active prompt's identity — and is passed to the card.
*   `lib/core/widgets/gateway_clarify_dialog.dart` — the card asks `canCloseRoute` before popping, so it only ever closes a route it still owns. The predicate defaults to owning the route, which keeps a card mounted as a route of its own closing itself.
*   `test/chat_clarify_batch_test.dart` — two ChatScreen-level regression tests. The first drives a two-question batch: answer the first, assert the chat survives, then answer the second. The second holds the `clarify.lock` in flight, cancels the request mid-send, and resolves the lock as `expired` while the card is still animating out.

## Verification

*   First test, pre-fix: fails with `Found 0 widgets with type "ChatScreen"` plus `'!_debugLocked': is not true` in `NavigatorState.build`; passes after the fix.
*   Second test, pre-fix (at `33bfa19`): fails with `Expected: exactly one matching candidate / Actual: _TypeWidgetFinder:<Found 0 widgets with type "ChatScreen": []>` — the late `expired` lock pops the chat screen; passes after the fix, and a later request is still presented and answered.
*   `flutter test` — 1275 passed (rebased onto `main` at v2.1.20).
*   `flutter analyze --no-pub --fatal-infos` — no issues found.
*   Not exercised on a physical device: this was written where no Android SDK or device was available.

Skip/dismiss paths are unaffected: by the time the drain sends its empty answer for a dismissed card, `_activeClarifyPrompt` is already null, so the reconcile returns early. A cancellation is unaffected on the answer path: the card's own pop is skipped once the route is no longer its own, and the drain already skips the empty answer for a cancelled request.

No `pubspec.yaml` or `CHANGELOG.md` change, so the CI versionCode base check stays intact.

**CI:** the `PR Quality Checks` run for this head is parked at `action_required` — GitHub gates workflow runs from forks until a maintainer approves them, so no status check is visible until then ([run 39142297450](https://github.com/rusty4444/hermes-android/actions/runs/39142297450)). Approving it is what makes the checks appear; the local run above is the same suite.

title: perf(android): show startup and Home sooner

## Summary

As each page arrives, fill up to five human chats even when the initial five API rows are cron; replace the preview with the complete list and Project/archive metadata. Later refreshes still fetch fresh sessions.
